Plead
pleed
v. (to argue a cause at law; to contend on behalf of or against; rendering Hebrew rib, Greek krino in the forensic sense)
From Old French plaidier, to go to law, from late Latin placitum, a decree or plea. Hebrew rib is a lawsuit or controversy — the prophets' standard form is the covenant lawsuit, in which God pleads against his people.

Biblical Definition

To plead in Scripture is a courtroom word, and God is the most frequent litigant. He pleads against his own people: “Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead” (Jeremiah 2:9) — the sentence is a summons, and the whole chapter is a covenant lawsuit charging Israel with exchanging a fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. Isaiah sets the scene formally: “The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people” (Isaiah 3:13) — and it is worth noting that God is described as standing, which in a courtroom is the posture of the advocate. He also commands the pleading of others' causes as a matter of religion: “Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isaiah 1:17). The widow's difficulty in an ancient court was that she had no man to speak for her, and God requires his people to be that man. The Psalter asks God to take the same office for the believer: “Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation” (Psalm 43:1) — a request that only makes sense because the Judge is also willing to be the Advocate, which is precisely what the New Testament says he is.

Webster 1828 Definition

To argue a cause at law. God pleads against his people in covenant lawsuit, commands his people to plead for the widow, and is asked to plead the believer's cause — being at once the Judge and the Advocate.

expand to see more

PLEAD, v.i. [Fr. plaider.] In a general sense, to argue in support of a claim, or in defense against the claim of another.

2. In law, to present an answer to the declaration of a plaintiff; to deny the plaintiff's declaration.

3. To urge reasons for or against; to attempt to persuade by argument or supplication.

4. PLEAD, v.t. To discuss and defend; as, to plead a cause.

5. To allege or adduce in proof, support or vindication; as, to plead one's cause; to plead the merits of Christ.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 2:9 — "Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead."

Isaiah 3:13 — "The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people."

Isaiah 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

Psalm 43:1 — "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man."

Modern Corruption

Advocacy for the defenceless is either abandoned to the state, or redefined by frameworks that assign standing by group rather than by the biblical categories of the widow, the fatherless, and the stranger.

expand to see more

Isaiah 1:17 names four duties and they are specific: seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. These are not abstractions but courtroom acts, and the persons named share one feature — they have no advocate. Two failures follow the loss of this. The first hands the whole matter to institutions, so that individual Christians no longer know a widow well enough to plead for anyone. The second replaces Scripture's categories with the oppressor-oppressed binary of critical race theory and related frameworks, in which standing is assigned by group identity rather than by actual defencelessness. Biblical anthropology has no room for that: all are one in Adam and, in Christ, one body, and Leviticus forbids partiality toward the poor as firmly as toward the mighty.

The principle to recover is that the Judge is the Advocate. Psalm 43:1 asks God both to judge and to plead, which would be a scandal in any human court and is the glory of the gospel. John states it plainly: if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1) — the word is parakletos, one called alongside to plead a cause. The believer stands before a bench where the one who will pass sentence has already argued his case and paid his fine, and this is why the Christian may ask to be judged rather than dreading it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rib is to contend, to conduct a lawsuit; the noun is a controversy or covenant lawsuit. Greek parakletos is one called alongside to plead, the Advocate.

expand to see more

Hebrew rib (H7378) — to strive, contend, plead a case; the verb of the prophetic covenant lawsuit.

Hebrew rib (H7379) — the noun: a controversy, a suit at law; the LORD hath a controversy with his people.

Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to pronounce sentence; paired with pleading in Isaiah 3:13.

Greek parakletos (G3875) — one called alongside; an advocate; of Christ and of the Holy Ghost.

Greek entugchano (G1793) — to intercede, to plead with; he ever liveth to make intercession.

Usage

"Of God's lawsuit with his people: I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD (Jeremiah 2:9)."

"Of the duty to the defenceless: judge the fatherless, plead for the widow (Isaiah 1:17)."

"Of the believer's request: judge me, O God, and plead my cause (Psalm 43:1)."
